FOUR MEN FOUND DEAD,
Two Hanging to a Tree and Two Shot Through.
The startling news reached the city yesterday that four dead men were found in Elm bottom yesterday morning, two of whom were hanging by their necks from limbs and two others pierced with bullets. The two hanging were about half a mile from the two found that were shot. The place is near the line of the Missouri Pacific road north of Lewisville. C. W. Hallsell, a young man, arrived in the city during the day and verified the rumor, yet the mail agent who came in on the 4 o'clock train from Denton, stated to a HERALD reporter that he had heard nothing of any bodies being found. Young Halsell says that Mrs. McWorter, who resides near Lewisville, gave him what little information he had, which was in substance as given above. None of the bodies, which were dressed in cow-boy style, were identified, yet one of the shot men was recognized as a party who had been seen the previous day at Caruth's ranch near where the remains had been found. Carter, a relative of Carter of Sam Bass fame, who is supposed to be one of the gang found dead, had been captured Tuesday night while trying to rob a passenger train on the Missouri Pacific road, several miles this side of Denton, but that he declared his ignorance as to whom the dead men were. The rumor lacks confirmation and is not credited.

Miss Mills, aged 17, Emma Oglesby, an orphan, aged 16, and Mary Jones, aged 14, all employed by Mr. Brown, who keeps a boarding-house, bought 25 cents' worth of arsenic, June 21, divided it into three doses, and swallowed it. MORE LYNCHING.
MORE LYNCHING.
The usually staid and law abiding parish of Bossier has been disgraced by a lynching affair. Tuesday night of last week a party of about a dozen men gained admission to the jailor's bedroom, obtained possession of the keys of the jail by threats, entered the prison and brought out Henry Solomon, a colored man, whom they hanged just outside the building. An inquest was held and, as usual, the jailor, his assistants and the prisoners incarcerated with Solomon all testified that they did not recognize any of the lynchers, though it does not even appear from the evidence, as reported by the Banner, that the law breakers were masked or disguised in any way.

Solomon had been imprisoned on a charge of mule stealing, and was thought to be a bad character, but it is not urged that he was ever convicted of any offense. During the night of the 10th inst., in company with one Jack Chapman, a white man convicted of murder and sentenced to death, Solomon broke out of jail and fled. The pair were subsequently captured and returned to prison. The night of the lynching the floor of the cell occupied by Solomon was found to be burning, and the prisoner is said to have acknowledged that he started the fire with the intention of effecting an escape. We presume this was the overt act that justified the lynchers, in their own estimation, in murdering a man who had never been convicted of any breach of law and was entitled to the legal presumption of innocence until proven guilty.

The Bossier Banner regrets the occurrence and says "such a method of inflicting justice is undoubtedly dangerous," but expresses "the candid belief that the legal quibbles and quirks so freely used in defense of criminals everywhere, now-a-days, is answerable for this state of affairs."

The excuse is a very weak one in this instance, for no attempt had yet been made under the forms of law to bring Solomon to an account for his alleged misdeeds. If the night-prowling jayhawkers were actuated by the fear that a criminal would escape punishment unless they inflicted it outside the pale of the law, why did they select a poor darkkey, never convicted of crime and only accused of stealing a mule, passing by a white murderer who had been duly tried and pronounced guilty and who is endeavoring to evade the penalty of his great crime—one of the most serious and infamous in the category of lawless deeds—by "legal quibbles and quirks?" Jake Chapman is prosecuting an appeal before the Supreme Court, and should any irregularity be discovered in the proceedings in his case, he will be granted a new trial and will stand the chance of securing an acquittal or of making a second and more successful attempt to escape by breaking jail and fleeing to parts unknown. If Solomon's effort to regain his liberty by flight is taken as a confession of guilt, the same assumption must apply in Chapman's case, even signifying the fact that the latter had been duly tried and convicted, while the former had never been accorded the right of a trial.

It certainly appears on the face of the record that the Bossier lynchers made a very marked distinction between white tweedle-dee and colored tweedle-dum, and in three out of every four instances of lynching in Louisiana the same tendency is to be observed. Notwithstanding the fact that the proportion of criminals who escape punishment in this State is fully three white to one colored, a considerable majority of those murdered by the outrageous methods of Judge Lynch are colored prisoners whose facilities for taking advantage of "legal quibbles and quirks" are far inferior to those of the white malefactor. On the 19th of December last, J. B. Weisinger, a plante, near Brown's station, Alabama, a man 60 years of age, was brutally murdered in his own house, half a dozen negroes being supposed to have had a hand in it. Two of them named Bill Ludlow and Al. Weisinger, were finally brought to trial and convicted, and on the 31st of March executed. Last night at about half past 10 o'clock it was reported on the streets that a man had been killed down in the first ward, at the house of ill-fame kept by Sallie Daggett. He remonstrated with them, whereupon they drew their six-shooters and threatened to kill him. Afterwards the colored man came to the city and reported the case to Officer John Watts, of the police force, who went in search of the men. They were traced to the house of ill-fame kept by Sallie Daggett, in the first ward. Their horses were found fastened in front of the house, and the officer, ascertaining that the men were upon the inside, went in to arrest them, summoning Mr. William McLellan to assist him. THE EVIDENCE.

Captain J. L. Watts, being sworn, testified: Last night about 11 o'clock I was informed, while on duty, that two white men had assaulted a colored man near Bertram's store, and that the unknown parties had gone towards the first ward. I went with the colored man that way, looking for the men, and came upon them in a house of ill-fame, known as Sallie Daggett's. Two heres were hitched in front, and recognized as the horses ridden by the men. I had a full description of the men. As I came to the gate I met Billie McCllan, and when inside I asked him to assist me in the arrest. Two of the girls, upon inquiry, said the men in question were in the wine room. I then crossed the little platform in the rear, leading to the said wine room, and met the two men aforesaid. I, approaching them, took each by the arm, saying: "Gentlemen, consider yourselves under arrest." Instantly both jumped back, drawing their pistols. I knocked the deceased off the steps, he having a pistol in his hand, and whirling to grab the other, one Jeff Ake, now present, the latter fired at me, striking me in the side. We began wrestling, and I observed the deceased again on his feet and advancing, aiming his pistol at me with both hands. I hallowed to McCllan, "For God's sake kill him!" He (McC.) said he had no pistol, and, upon my request, quickly took mine from my belt, as I could not get away from Jeff Ake. McCllan fired upon the deceased. When I succeeded in getting Jeff Ake to the door and throwing him I learned from McCllan that the deceased was shot. The prisoner had fired a second shot, ineffectually, at me, while the tussle was continuing. Upon the appearance of the city marshal, in answer to summons through others, coming upon the scene, I left with Jeff Ake in custody. Above happened on 2nd day of January, A. D., 1883.

AN INTERVIEW WITH JEFF AKES IN JAIL.

A STATESMAN reporter called at the jail yesterday afternoon at 5 o'clock, and requested an interview with Jeff Akes, when Captain A. Denny, the efficient keeper of the prison, courteously showed him up to the cell where the prisoner is confined.

HIS APPEARANCH.

The prisoner is a man of probably thirty-five years of age, five feet six inches high, rather sparely made, and has light or sandy hair. His eye is dull and uninteresting, but the whole contour of his face, as well as his decided expression and precise manner, would seem to indicate decision of character. In fact, his very looks betoken a "bad man," when aroused or under the influence of drink. When informed that a reporter wished to see him, Akes, who was reclining upon a pallet upon the floor, slowly and deliberately arose, seemingly indifferent as to whether he got up or not. His manner toward the interviewer, however, was very civil and might even be called pleasant. His replies to interrogatories put to him were prompt and, apparently, without reservation. He denied most emphatically that he attacked the negro man as stated, and accounts for the assertion upon the theory that he was mistaken for some one else.

HIS STORY

of the fight is to the effect that he and his companion were drinking, and visited the house where the difficulty occurred simply "upon a lark." He says that when Mr. Watts approached him he did not know he (Watts) was an officer, and had he been duly apprised of the fact no resistance would have been made. Two Men Hanged by a Mob in Elliott County. [Grayson (Ky.) Cor. Cincinnati Enquirer.]

Murder, incendiarism, thievery, bushwhacking, general devilment—and such a farce as most of the Kentucky courts prove to be when criminals are brought before them—have at last incited the better citizens of Northeast Kentucky to rise in their might and enforce their will as best they can. In dispatches some weeks since mention was made of an organized band of outlaws in this part of Kentucky, and that a body of masked men had visited Martinsburg, the county seat of Elliott county, and served notices on officers, lawyers, citizens and criminals that they would no longer suffer murderers and known criminals to override and disgrace their county, and that officers and lawyers who gave them encouragement by defending and permitting such persons to go unpunished would be served in the same way as criminals.

On Monday near midnight about 200 men rode into the town of Martinsburg and surrounded the entire court-yard, in which the jail stands, in which John W. Kendall, William McMillan and J. W. Ownsby were confined, charged with various crimes, and known to belong to the organization holding sway in this part of the State. In the meantime part of the regulators surrounded the jailer's house, from which he attempted to escape by a back door, but, in the darkness, ran into the arms of one of the party. They made him deliver the keys to the jail. When they surrounded the court-yard there were several men about the yard with the guards. Among them was John Cohn, whom they caught and tried to secure, but he broke away from them. They fired two shots at him, both of which took effect, one in the left shoulder, the other in the left hip. He finally escaped. They intended to hang him. The party having the jail keys arrived by this time, when about twenty-five proceeded to the jail. Unlocking it, they were met by William McMillan, who began praying for mercy. Kendall was stolid, and made no appeals. Ownsby talked but little, but he was badly frightened, as he had been hanged several times some weeks since by the regulators to make him tell what he knew of the band that he belonged to. Only one man spoke to him. They soon produced ropes and pinioned the arms of Kendall and McMillan, and, leading them to the door, placed the ropes around their necks. They left Ownsby praying for mercy, closed and locked the door, laid the keys by the side of the door, and, without a word being spoken by the whole party of men, filed out of the courtyard and proceeded to a walnut tree about 100 yards from the Court House, where they formed a hollow square about their prisoners and instituted a trial bench. After near an hour the sentence of death was pronounced by Judge Lynch. McMillan begged for a little time to pray, which was granted. A small rope that had evidently been used as a plow-line was used to hang McMillan. When all was ready four strong men caught him and held him up some distance so that one of the party, who climbed the tree, could tie the rope to a limb. They let him down gradually, so as not to break the rope. He was strangled to death. Until this time Kendall had kept quiet. When he saw his partner in the throes of death, he began calling on his God for mercy. His prayers were cut short. He died hard. Both were hanged on the same tree. The regulators remained about half an hour, and quietly left town by another road.

It is a wild and gloomy spot, if you follow the boundaries of the plateau and view it from the opposite bank of the river. Walled in on all sides by frowning cliffs, rising nearly perpendicular to the height of 300 feet, their upper edge fringed by a heavy growth of stunted firs and laurel bushes, it certainly has a forbidding look. If you have the curiosity to explore the plateau and climb the summit of the crumbling cliff at the point of jointure with the mainland, the aspect changes. Ten years ago there was a thick growth of heavy timber on the "neck," but it has all been cleared away, and a vista of fertile fields and neatly fenced plantations sweep away on all sides to the cliff edges, which are still bordered by the laurel and fir growth. Evidences of civilization in the way of comfortable houses and stables and sheep flocks cropping the succulent herbage are seen on every hand. Immediately after the close of the late war a man named Peter J. Livingstone, who had commanded a regimen of guerrillas on the Confederate side, purchased the neck for a nominal sum, cleared away the timber, laid off fields, built roads and erected houses and opened a store just on the verge of the crumbling cliff, down which you clambered to reach the mainland. He cut down this cliff and graded a road to the farther edge of the plateau, with lateral feeders running off on either side. He brought his family here, installed them in a luxurious home, and began a flourishing business, the basis of which was timber, great tracts of which were owned by him on the mainland. The geographical situation of the "neck" was an admirable one for business purposes, it being a sort of half-way station between the undeveloped riches of wild Kentucky and capital which stretched out eager hands toward the new-old country from the other side of the Ohio river. He speedily drew about him an enormous trade and acted as a factor for the whole of the back country. He was an affable, pleasant-mannered man and made friends.
At this time Mountain Kentucky was in a state of anarchy, Law and order were but little regarded, and the woods were filled with armed men engaged in those terrible family feuds which have made the dark and bloody ground famous. It was the favorite rendezvous, too, for a much worse class of criminals. Thieves and counterfeiters made their headquarters among the wild gorges and deep forests from which they emerged, at frequent intervals, to prey on the fatness of the rich blue-grass country but a few miles distant. Robberies were of frequent occurrence, and stolen horses and cattle were stamped out of the low country by the hundred head. They would be secreted here until the hue and cry was over, and then conveyed across the Ohio river and sold. It was known to the authorities that the desperadoes were well organized, and all efforts to break up the gang were fruitless. During all this time Colonel Peter J. Livingstone flourished and waxed rich, and no one suspected that he had a hand in the lawless acts which were fast driving honest people out of the mountains, and deterring others from coming in to take their places.

Peter J. Livingstone's business prospered so well that it was not long before he had competition. Two Virginians, father and son, named Malone, set up a store on the mainland, directly on the road to Livingstone's store, and much of the trade which hitherto of necessity had gone to him was directed to the new establishment. The falling off in his business enraged Colonel Livingstone beyond measure, and he had an open quarrel with the Malones. After this quarrel the two firms tried to injure each other in the way of trade as much as possible. Livingstone made threats that he would break up the Malones, and drive them from the county. In the spring of 1877 Malone's store was broken into and robbed of several hundred dollars' worth of goods, and Colonel Livingstone gloried in the discomfiture of his rivals over their loss. A few months afterwards a fire broke out in Malone's store, but was happily extinguished before much damage was done. After this second misfortune one of Malone's clerks, a
john-binion-elliott-county-1882-06.A17: The story of this execution, "by command of Judge Lynch," is a brief one. The two secret meetings which had been held by the citizens of Elliott county, were for the purpose of organizing a "society of public protection and justice." One of the most prominet citizens of the county was at its head. Every man of standing, every man who loved order and respected the law in the county enrolled himself in the new order. Its spies were more ubiquitous than the hired detective, and brought to the chief of the order startling intelligence. Livingstone's gang was becoming frightened, and had resolved on heroic measures for the succor of their brethren in durance vile. They had resolved to anticipate the law's slow delay, and rescue their friends by force. At the same time it was intended to burn Martinsburg and shoot down all opposition. The generalissimo of the "Regulators" knew that Peter J. Livingstone was at the head of the order. He had wrung a confirmation of this knowledge from Ormsby and from Kendall and McMillan. He was provided with a list of the members of the gang. The lodge, in solemn conclave, voted to mete out impartial justice to all evil doers. Sentence of death was pronounced on Kendall, McMillan, Livingstone, Lewis Binion, John Binion and John Boggs. Other members of the gang received sentences varying from five to one hundred lashes on the bare back and notice to quit the State. The lodge rode into Martinsburg at midnight, armed and disguised; they forced the jailer to deliver up the keys of the jail, and brought forth Kendall and McMillan to suffer the extreme penalty of lynch law. The frightened wretches confessed everything, implicated Livingstone, the two Binions and Boggs, and were hung up to a walnut tree in the Court House yard. A proclamation was posted in
john-binion-elliott-county-1882-06.A18:
several prominent places threatening evil doers and their friends and sympathizers with the vengeance of the Regulators.

After hanging the two prisoners the band quietly dispersed. The execution created considerable excitement, but no effort was made to bring the lynchers to justice. The night following they captured Louis Binion and hung him to a ladder set up against his own house. Others of the gang were visited and whipped and ordered to leave the state. For a month the Regulators were every night whipping and hanging. John Binion took to the "bush," and one night endeavored to get out of the county. He and Boggs were to leave together. The latter was a hunter and fisherman, and the place of rendezvous of the two proscribed men was a log cabin which Boggs sometimes occupied on his hunting excursions. The Regulators learned of the movements of the two men and sought to check their flight. They surrounded the cabin and demanded an unconditional surrender. Binion and Boggs refused to give themselves up. The Regulators fired a volley into the cabin, broke down the door, shot Boggs dead and wounded Binion. Binion begged for mercy, but they laughed his prayer to scorn. A rope was placed about his neck, and howling and praying he was dragged to the nearest tree. They strung him up, and as he writhed under the cruel, choking rope, fired a volley into the swinging body and ended the wretch's misery.

The arch criminal Livingstone, however, escaped them. It appears that he learned of the hanging of the two men in Martinsburg and their betrayal of him that same night, and making hasty preparations he fled across the Big Sandy into West Virginia. He remained in hiding for several weeks, wound up his business, collected together all the ready money he could realize and went to Texas, in one of the frontier towns of which state he is now located. The rest of the gang fled the state. A great deal of stolen property was recovered by the detective and returned to the owners. The property on "Cracker's Neck" was divided up and sold by Livingstone's son, after which the young man went to Texas to join his sire.

The new order increased its membership and established subordinate lodges in other counties. It restored order and made law respected. It drove out the desperadoes, thieves and outlaws, and made it possible for an honest man to live in Elliott county. As an evidence of what terror of evil-doing was inspired by the Regulators it is said that a man could lay down a thousand dollars in the middle of the road anywhere in the county and leave it there for weeks without fear of its being picked up, because, as a mountaineer quaintly expressed it to the writer :

"Thar's no tellin', mister, how many rifles mought be coverin' thet same thousand' dollahs, nor how quick a man mought see kingdom kum. Who'd be dratted fool enuff to pick hit up?" —[Detroit Free Press.

Bloodshed in Lake County.
OFTLAND. March 12th.—The Oreax
Bloodshed in Lake County.
PORTLAND, March 12th.—The Oregonian's Jacksonville special says: Last night at 10 o'clock ten or twelve masked men rode into Linkville, where A. C. Laws, charged with the murder of Frank Calavan, was in custody of Deputy Sheriff J. F. Lewis and Justice Wright awaiting examination before the latter, which was to take place Monday. The officers were in Greenman's Hotel with the prisoner when the lynchers entered the hall and were ordered to halt. The lynchers refused, and Lewis fired his revolver, wounding one of the party slightly. The lynchers returned the fire, killing the Deputy Sheriff and wounding Justice Wright. They then left without taking Laws. The excitement is intense, and the feeling in Langell valley is very strong against Laws.
laws-linkville-1882-03-11.A4:
LAWLESS DESPERADOES IN LAKE COUNTY.
George Law, who murdered the Calavan boy, on February 13th, about ten miles east of Langell valley, in vicinity of the State line between Modoc and Lake counties, which we mentioned several days ago, is a noted desperado, and chief of the Bonanza Regulators, an organization to prevent settlers from locating in the vicinity of Bonanza. Other persons have been killed suspiciously on former occasions, chargeable to these regulators, who seem to govern that portion of Lake county with as much terror as the cowboys in Arizona. The father of these boys was clubbed sometime ago, and just before an old man was found murdered in his cabin, who had taken up some land for a home. The two boys, when accosted by Law, expected trouble, as threats had been previously made, and the older boy, age 19, had his pistol cocked as quick as Law had his Winchester cocked, both firing instantly, though the younger boy, aged 15, said before his death that Law fired first. Law followed the boys for a fight, as they were not disturbing him, and only looking on the feed grounds for some of their missing cattle. The oldest boy fired his revolver six times at Law, in return for as many rifle shots, and then told his younger brother, who was unarmed, to run his horse at full speed for home, as he had no shots left. As the boy started Law commenced shooting at him, and noticing he was wounded, the older boy sung out to him to let go the bridle rein and hang to the saddle, the latter taking to the brush, as his horse was wounded and unable to travel. The elder Calavan boy felt a bullet pass close by his cheek while in the brush, supposed to be young Law's rifle, and hanging his coat in the brush as a blind he managed to crawl away and escape to his cabin, where the younger brother had pulled off his boots and appeared to be in a dying condition, though able to talk. The elder boy then procured medical assistance from Langell valley, but could not save him. A large posse of citizens, about a dozen or more, headed by the Constable of Bonanza, started to Law's place to arrest him. The Constable thought it best for only three of them to go to Law's place, as he might otherwise show fight. Accordingly they succeeded in making the arrest, but young Law, aged about 20, got the drop on the officer, compelling him to surrender, and, wheeling around quickly, obliged the other two men to do the same. Young Law, assisted by his father and two other persons, after causing the Constable and the two citizens to leave, concluded to follow them, and run them down to where the balance of the citizens were secreted, who, having formed themselves into a circle, succeeded in securing young Law and two other men named Gordon and McKillen, the old man getting away. The elder Law was defiant, and said he would not be taken alive, though it is said he has given himself up, and was bound over by the Bonanza Justice, the others being discharged. There seems to be some doubt whether the murder was committed in Oregon or California. There is a strong feeling against these regulators in both Lake and Modoc counties, and the necks of Law and others will not be safe from Judge Lynch if they can be caught away from their stronghold.—[Yreka Journal, March 8th.

laws-linkville-1882-03-11.A16:
Tragical Tales.
At a dance at the house of John Mooney, in Indian Territory, on the night of the 10th inst., two young men named Montgomery and Horton got into a quarrel, which ended in both drawing pistols and shooting several times at each other. Montgomery was killed outright and Horton mortally wounded.

Two laborers named Monahan and MacAvoy quarreled at Steubenville, O., on the 11th inst. The latter was fatally stabbed.

At Linkville, Oregon, on the night of the 11th inst., a mob of masked men attempted to take a murderer named H. C. Lewis from the jail. Lewis fired on the mob, who responded with a volley, which killed the deputy sheriff and wounded Justice Wright. The would-be lynchers then retired.

A terrible tragedy was enacted at a school house at Harrisburg, Pernsett County, Ark., on the 7th inst. County Treasurer J. J. Smith remonstrated with the teacher for whipping his child. The conversation became heated and finally led to Smith's striking E. J. Wilmot, the teacher, on the head with a billet of wood, crushing his skull. The injured man died in three hours.

In a drunken quarrel at New Orleans on the night of the 7th inst., Richard Shea was stabbed to death by James Cosgrove.

An aged couple named O'Massey, living near Charlottesville, Va., were found murdered on the morning of the 8th inst., in their house. Money was the object.

A mob took Charles Shelton, John Redmond and Harry French from the jail at Los Lunas, Cal., on the 8th inst., and hung them to a tree.

A courtesan named Mary Sigman and her mother were assassinated at Mount Vernon, Ky., on the 8th inst.

A remarkable story comes from the City of Mexico. The report is that highwaymen attacked a stage full of armed men and that eleven of the outlaws were killed.

It is reported that nine Europeans journeying from Tunis to Gafsa were murdered between Tunis and Kairwan.

Advices from New Mexico are to the effect that Deputy Sheriff Miers and Martinez with a posse were attacked by Pueblo Indians while attempting to arrest some of the Pueblos who had escaped from jail. Miers was killed and Martinez mortally wounded.

A shocking tragedy took place at Boston, Mass., on the 7th inst. Mrs. Harriet Bell while returning from a grocery store near her home was accosted by an unknown man who followed her to the doorstep of her home and then cut her throat. She lived but a short time. The assassin escaped.

A brace of cattle thieves named Arnold Howard and Frank Young, in jail at Del Noter, Col., were visited by a mob on the 7th inst. Howard was killed outright and Young mortally wounded.

An affray with pistols took place at Arkansas City, on the 5th inst., in which J. W. Hale was killed by John Fuller.

Three negroes—Lewis Smith and Aaron and Ed. Clark—were killed in an affray at Arkadelphia, Ark., on the 6th inst. The shooting was done by Joe Ross and Thad. Henry, both white.

Tax Collector Robert Taylor was shot dead by Dr. Sims at Perryville, Perry County, Ark., on the 4th inst.

laws-linkville-1882-03-11.A25:
COAST AND STATE.
Redwood creek and harbor, in San Mateo county, are complaining of the debris filling them up, and asking our uncle to dredge them out.

The Vallejo Odd Fellows have decided to celebrate the coming anniversary of their Order by an excursion on April 26th to Fairfax Park, near San Rafael, in Marin county, and have engaged the steamer San Rafael for the trip.

The San Jose Mercury says: The numerous attempts made during the past three months to burn the churches of this city, one of which at last proved successful, would seem to indicate there is a crank running loose who is greatly in need of a little judicious killing.

Salmon are now beginning to run pretty plentifully, and the run will increase for several weeks. From fifty to a hundred boats are now engaged in the Straits fisheries, catching an average of twenty to thirty salmon a day. A larger number will soon be employed, and the average catch per boat will be larger during the next two months. —[Contra Costa Gazette.

The farmers in the neighborhood of Vallejo and Benicia are much pleased with the present prospects of large crops. The season was so favorable that almost every available acre of land was put in, and if the weather continues favorable a larger crop will be harvested than ever before. On account of so much land being sown with grain the hay crop will be very short, and it is thought that some of the grain will have to be cut for hay.

The Lakeview (Or.) Examiner says that the men who composed the mob that attempted to lynch Laws at Linkville, and in the melee killed Deputy Sheriff Lewis, are all Lassen county men, and live in and around Beiber and Big Valley. The Examiner gives a detailed account of the fracas, which, if true, shows that the lynchers acted in a cowardly and cold-blooded manner. They all broke and ran for the brush after killing an officer who was powerless in their hands, he at the time he was shot crouching down under cover of a mobber's shotgun.

A meeting of the Seattle, Puget Sound and Gray's Harbor Railroad and Transportation Company was held in Seattle. The President, Governor Newell, and other members of the Board were present. A report was received from the engineer who had made a survey over the proposed route, which represented that the grading and trestle work would be comparatively small. The location of termini on Puget Sound and harbor were not definitely settled. Steilacoom, Johnson's, Dofflamyer's and Brown's points and Olympia were carefully discussed, but no conclusion reached. The road will be about fifty miles in length, passing through one of the very best and most extensive regions of fir, cedar and spruce timber in Washington Territory, along the valley of the Chehalis, well known as one of the most fertile valleys of the Sound country, already highly cultivated and thickly inhabited. It was resolved unanimously to press the enterprise vigorously, and, if possible, to secure an early construction of the road.
laws-linkville-1882-03-11.A26: The people of Lakeview are determined to try and secure the arrest of persons connected with the mob at Linkville. The Commissioners have offered $1,000 reward, and the citizens intend subscribing another $1,000 to secure at least two or more. Should that many be found, it is believed the rest may be found out, all of whom will no doubt be indicted for the murder of Deputy Sheriff Lewis. The Oregonians claim that the mob comprised Californians from Big Valley, and the Big Valley people say they were friends of Laws endeavoring to get Laws from custody under pretense of desiring to lynch him. The latter charge, however, is not generally believed, but it is a matter of doubt whether the mob consisted of Oregonians or Californians, and may have comprised both, as Laws was a terror to the people along the boundary line, where several murders committed are charged to him and the Bonanza regulators, of which organization he was the chief.—[Yreka Journal.
laws-linkville-1882-03-11.A28:
A Travetsy on Justice.
For some cause the grand jury of Moloc county, Cal., did not find an indictment against H. C. Laws, who killed young Calavan near the State line sometime since. This is a surprise and has occasioned a deal of public indignation.

The affair becoming known, a warrant was procured for the arrest of the negroes atacking, Weaver, and placed in the hands of Mr. Sam Hunt to execute. On being approached by Hunt, one of the negroes drew a pistol and attempted to shoot, but Hunt, seeing his effo. t, fired first, killing the negro instantly. Hunt, it is said, has fled. The other negroes concerned in the affair have been arrested and placed in jail at this place. Their names are Bill Head and Jim Higgins.

We clip the following local item from the Macon Graphic: "Workmen are blasting away at the foot of Third street, in order to straighten the line of the East Tennessee, Virginia and Georgia Railroad in that locality, and for the additional purpose of securing ground for a passenger station. The work is necessarily slow and tedious, as a strata of stone underlies all the earth in that vicinity. The heavy explosions heard in that portion of the city comes from the discharge of these powder mines. The undertaking is a great one, but gradually the hilt is disappearing and the tops of debris and dirt excavated is being moved along the line to strengthen weak places and perfect the roadbed. When finished, the passenger depot at that point will be very attractive both from the fine tree growth thereabouts and the unusual water vista presented, up and down the Ocmulgee."

At Mandan, Dakota, on a trestle-work sixty feet high, a fight occurred between William Watson, of Saginaw, Mich., and Peter P. Stnart, of Dall Prairie, Mich., which ended in both going over to death with their arms clinched.

Robert Helding and John Robertson, Swedes, were arrested for petty thieving at Chicago, on the 13th inst. tom-law-rockmart-1882-07-15.A14:
A BLOODY FIGHT.
One Man Killed and Several Wounded.
A bloody fight occurred at the railroad tunnel in Paulding county, seven miles from Rockmart, on last Saturday afternoon. Mr. Geo. Foote keeps a bar room at that place, where negro laborers on the Macon and Brunswick extension congregated at night, fiddled, danced and drank whiskey. A white man named John Hicks, a quarrelsome rowdy, lived in the neighborhood, and his frequent visits to this greggery resulted in several disturbances with the negroes. On Thursday some farmers carried a wagon loud of peaches and watermelons to the camps to sell. During the sale, one of the farmers accused a negro boy of stealing some of the fruit. This highly incensed the negroes, who flourished their pistols and made some bold threats. The farmers whipped up their horses and started off, and fired a shot gun at the negroes. A running fight ensued and some fifty shots were fired. The farmers were crowded so closely that they had to jump from the wagon and take to the woods. This caused the horses to run away, smashing the wagon.

Saturday afternoon, John Hicks and his little son, entered the bar room where the negroes were dancing and proceeded to disarm the negroes of their pistols, falsely representing himself to be an officer. Several gave up their pistols, but one negro stoutly refused, and exchanged shots with Hicks. The negro was hit and fell mortally wounded. This was the beginning of a general fight and Hicks was riddled with bullets, some of the negroes shooting him several times after he was dead. Foote had to flee for his life, but he was slightly wounded in the heel and arm. Several negroes were wounded, and one has since died. After the killing of Hicks, the negroes took possession of the bar room and cleaned it out.

On Sunday the Sheriffs of Paulding and Polk counties, with a posse, visited the camps to suppress further trouble and to arrest those engaged in the fight. At first the negroes defied the officers, being well armed with new pistols bought from the railroad commissary. But the Sheriff's posse were armed with shot guns and had them surrounded, and the negroes seeing resistance would bring on a bloody conflict, they surrendered, and 25 of them were arrested and carried to Dallas and put in jail. On a preliminary trial doubtless some of them will be released. At the railroad camps on Monday all hands resumed work and it is probably no further trouble will ensue, although the feeling excited is very bitter. The officers are vigilant in their efforts to arrest all concerned in the affray.

A WAR OF RACES

A Row in Georgia Between Whites and Blacks—One White Man and a Negro Killed and Six Colored Men Wounded.

ATLANTA, Ga., July 17.—Two men who were compelled to leave Polk county on account of the passage of the "option law," established a saloon at the mouth of the tunnel being constructed on the Mason & Brunswick extension railroad, Paulding county. The railroad authorities have used every endeavor to get rid of the great annoyance, but to no purpose. Those who have generally frequented this place have been white men and desperate characters. A short time ago Hagan, employed in getting timber, went there to get cheese and crackers, when John Hicks got into a quarrel with him and shot him. Wednesday last the proprietor of the saloon went to camp and into the commissary with two revolvers, searching for one of the hands, whom he found and shot at, saying this man had informed revenue officers against him. A few days ago some of these men went into the camp armed with revolvers and shot-guns, ostensibly to sell peaches. Whilst trading they accused one of the negroes of stealing some of their peaches, and pointed a gun at him, as they said, to make him disgorge. Their conduct caused a crowd to gather, when they left. A short distance off one of them turned and fired at the crowd, when the fire was returned, and the running fire was kept up between the negroes and the peach sellers, in which some fifty shots were fired. Friday morning Hicks, the desperado, went to camp armed with two revolvers and with a box of catridges in his pocket. Saturday (pay day) John Hicks again came to the camp armed, and attempted to disarm the negroes, many of whom had armed themselves for self-protection. Hicks succeeded in disarming some four or five of the negroes, he was resisted by one man, and a fight ensued. This was at the mouth of the tunnel where the saloon is located. In the fight Hicks and one negro were killed and six negroes were wounded, Hicks receiving eight balls in his body. The negroes succeeded in driving the whites from the saloon, of which they remained in possession until yesterday noon. On Saturday night the sheriff of Paulding county was notified and assembled a posse, and went immediately to the tunnel, where the sheriff of Polk county also assembled his posse. The negroes first refused to surrender, but afterwards submitted to the arrest of those engaged in the disturbance, and the remainder quietly dispersed.

THE United States Fish Commission has made a special report to Congress, which will be the most exhaustive work on food fishes ever printed. It will make three quarto volumes of eight hundred pages each, and be profusely illustrated.

At a meeting of the Ohio Republican Association in Washington, D. C., the other night, a letter from Mrs. Garfield, offering to sell the family residence, at the corner of Thirteenth and I streets, was read. She set forth that she preferred to have the place fall into the hands of such an association, which would cherish it for the memories connected with it, rather than let it go to some private party who might alter it. She said that Gen. Garfield had told her once that it was worth $18,000, but she would take $15,000 for it. Real estate dealers value the property at $9,000.

PARTICULARS of a riot between colored railway laborers and some whites living near Carterville, Ga., have just been received. Several weeks since a white man named Hicks, a desperado, shot at several railroad hands for slight cause. The other day a party of whites went to a store in the neighborhood with peaches to sell, and while trading a negro boy was charged with stealing some fruit. One of the whites aimed a gun at him, but did not fire; but after leaving the store one of the fruit peddlers turned and fired into a group of negro workmen, who returned the fire and pursued the whites, about fifty shots being exchanged but no one hurt. The next day Hicks quarreled with a number of the negro hands who were gathered at the store, disarming five, and was in the act of disarming a sixth when the negro, resisting, was shot and killed. This tragedy wrought up the negroes to the highest excitement, and forming a mob they attacked Hicks with great ferocity. He ran for his life, but before he had got fifty yards away was literally riddled with bullets. More whites appeared upon the ground and four negroes were badly wounded, but the former soon fled before superior numbers, and the negroes patroled the counties of Paulding and Polk all night and the next day, defying two sheriffs and a posse.

At De Soto, Mo., July 16, John Casey stabbed and killed Oliver Sauburg, a section foreman of the Iron Mountain Road. The cause of the murder is unknown. Casey is under arrest.

A Murderer Arrested.
Sheriff W. C. Matthews, of Paulding County, Ga., took the noon train here Monday, having in charge Wm. Slaughter, colored, arrested in Campbell County, and being taken back to Georgia to be tried for his connection with a riot. This riot occurred on the Cincinnati and Georgia Railroad works, at Tunnel Hill, about the middle of July last. One of the contractors, Mr. McKeckney, had a large force of colored hands, and he armed them with pistols, for what purpose it is not known to us. On Saturday evening, John Hicks, a citizen of that vicinity who had been employed as a boss, undertook to disarm the men. He succeeded in getting two or three of their pistols, but at that time a riot ensued, and one of the negroes, named Gabe, whom Hicks was trying to disarm, was badly wounded. About this time some 300 of the negroes, armed, came up and began a promiscuous shooting. Hicks stood his ground and shot as long as his ammunition lasted, when he and his two little boys broke to run, but were followed, and Hicks was literally riddled with bullets, his boys interceding for his life.

The news was telegraphed to Sheriff Matthews, at Dallas, the county seat, that night, and he reached the spot the next morning with a posse of men. He was joined by the sheriff of Polk county, with some men, and they arrested thirty-three of the men, identified as having been engaged in the riot. They were afterwards tried, five were sent to the penitentiary for life, and the rest for twelve months each.

Wm. Slaughter was the leader of the riot. He, with one or two others of the instigators, escaped. Slaughter came from Virginia and is a desperate looking fellow, of pretty powerful make, and very black. Sheriff Matthews, with the exercise of considerable skill as an officer, finally succeeded, by correspondence, in tracing and locating Slaughter on the railroad works of Capt. J. L. Offutt, in Elk Valley, Campbell County, and about the 18th of September, Deputy Sheriff J. P. Hollingsworth, of Campbell County, by instructions, identified and arrested him, and lodged him in the Jacksboro jail. Sheriff Matthews procured the necessary requisition papers, came last Saturday evening and went to Jacksboro and secured his prisoner. He brought him on yesterday's Ohio division train, safely menacled, and was accompanied this far by Sheriff J. L. Smith, of Campbell County.
